research.abstract: Abstract Red algae produce structurally diverse haloterpenoids unique to seaweeds, yet the enzymes responsible for generating many of their core terpene scaffolds remain unknown. Here, we report the identification of red algal UbiA-type terpene synthases (UTSs), a noncanonical enzyme family recently associated with terpene biosynthesis in bacteria and fungi. By prioritizing UbiA candidates located near putative biosynthetic genes, we identified eight candidate gene clusters across two red algal species, Laurencia pacifica and Laurencia subopposita . Using the heterologous host plant Nicotiana benthamiana , we show that the UbiA genes act as non-canonical TSs and that two UTSs produce the sesquiterpene bisabolene. The discovery of the bisabolene UTSs, LsUTS-2 and LpUTS-2, lays the foundation for laurane and chamigrane-type sesquiterpenoid production, addressing a prior biosynthetic quandary that bisabolene is not produced by established red algal class I TSs. Phylogenetic analyses distinguish the red algal UTSs from canonical UbiA prenyltransferases involved in primary metabolism and suggest they were acquired outside the red algal lineage. These findings expand the known distribution of UTSs and establish a previously unrecognized route to red algal terpene scaffolds.

research.abstract: Tsaoko stripe mosaic virus (TkSMV) has been identified as the predominant viral pathogen of Amomum tsaoko in Yunnan Province of China. This virus induced various foliar symptoms, including chlorosis, stripe mosaic, and necrosis, while some infected A. tsaoko plants remain asymptomatic. Comprehensive investigation of the population genetic structure and molecular detection protocols for TkSMV is crucial for elucidating its evolutionary dynamics, epidemiology, and disease control strategies. Phylogenetic analysis based on 15 full-length genomic sequences and 29 coat protein (CP) gene fragments revealed three distinct evolutionary lineages (S1, S2, and S3) within the TkSMV population. Neutrality test analysis indicates that the genetic polymorphism of the TkSMV population is consistent with a neutral evolution model (Tajima’s D > 0, not significant). The comparative evolutionary analysis demonstrated significant selective pressures across viral proteins: codon usage bias analysis revealed strong purifying selection (dN/dS < 1) in nine structural/functional proteins, eliminating deleterious mutations. The 9K gene exhibited the highest nucleotide diversity (π = 0.13567), suggesting its role in adaptive evolution. NIa-Pro protease showed the lowest diversity (π = 0.09497), indicating functional constraint. Remarkably, the CP gene displayed polarized evolutionary patterns. The N-terminal region (amino acids 1 to 100) acted as a hypervariable hotspot, while the C-terminal region (amino acids 151 to 240) maintained evolutionary conservation. Furthermore, multiplex RT-PCR assays for accurate discrimination of TkSMV-S1/S2/S3 strains in mixed infections were developed. These advancements provide a technical foundation for epidemiological surveillance through strain-specific monitoring and seed certification programs for A. tsaoko cultivation.

research.abstract: Background Anterior chest wall tuberculosis is an uncommon form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that can mimic a chronic pyogenic abscess or chest wall mass. Its indolent presentation and absence of constitutional symptoms may delay diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. Case presentation A 22-year-old previously healthy male soldier presented with a progressively enlarging parasternal-xiphoid swelling and intermittent seropurulent discharge, without respiratory or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed a minimally tender 5 × 2 cm fluctuant swelling with a draining sinus and localized skin changes. Thoracic computed tomography showed a 57 × 18 mm subcutaneous collection at the xiphoid level without demonstrated pleural or osseous involvement, alongside centrilobular nodules and a tree-in-bud pattern suggestive of pulmonary infection. Incision, drainage, and debridement were performed. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing of a fluid specimen detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex at a low bacillary load, without rifampicin resistance detected. Histopathological examination was reported to show caseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Sputum testing was also positive for M. tuberculosis, supporting concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis. First-line antituberculous therapy was initiated. The wound was closed at the 14-day postoperative assessment. Following six months of treatment, the patient remained asymptomatic; follow-up computed tomography demonstrated resolution of the chest wall collection and regression of pulmonary abnormalities. Conclusion Chest wall tuberculosis should be considered in patients with persistent parasternal swelling or a draining sinus, even without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Tissue sampling, molecular and histopathological evaluation, and assessment for concomitant pulmonary disease support timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

research.abstract: Alzheimers disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) are clinical disorders characterized by declines in cognitive function to levels at which everyday living is meaningfully impaired. Genetic variants may confer risk for AD/ADRD by way of steeper rates of aging-related cognitive declines or their association with lower premorbid levels of cognitive function that place individuals closer to a clinically severe threshold of cognitive function. We applied joint longitudinal-hazard models to 26-year data from an ancestrally diverse US sample of N = 11,518 adults to estimate effects of multi-ancestry polygenic indices (PGIs) for a range of established risk factors on dementia hazard and the degree they operate via premorbid cognitive function and longitudinal cognitive decline. APOE e4 and PGIs for ADRD, type 2 diabetes, stroke, LDL cholesterol, and hearing loss operated via rate of change, whereas PGIs for educational attainment, cognitive function, physical activity, BMI, smoking, loneliness, schizophrenia, and externalizing were associated with dementia hazard via premorbid differences in cognitive function. Some results varied by continental ancestry. Our implementation of joint longitudinal-hazard models allowed us to distinguish how different genetic risk factors for AD/ADRD operate via degenerative processes that might be therapeutically targeted during later life and via premorbid levels of cognitive function that would require intervention earlier in the life course.

research.abstract: Background: Albuminuria testing to diagnose chronic kidney disease (CKD) and guide blood pressure management is recommended for adults with hypertension but remains underused in part due to suboptimal patient understanding of its importance. Patient facing behavioral interventions have the potential to bridge this gap. We developed and evaluated KnowCKD, a behaviorally informed intervention designed to increase patient awareness of CKD and knowledge and promote albuminuria testing among adults with hypertension. Methods: KnowCKD consisted of an educational infographic and brief, behaviorally informed messages delivered to patients' smartphones during the 5 days leading up to and including a scheduled primary care visit at one academic medical center. Among 57 adults with hypertension without diabetes or recent albuminuria testing, we assessed changes in CKD awareness and knowledge and patient-reported engagement via survey pre- and post- exposure to KnowCKD. Electronic Health Record (EHR)- confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing was compared with 182 contemporaneous primary care controls using unmatched and propensity score-matched analysis. A postintervention focus group evaluated participant experiences. Results: After exposure to KnowCKD, recognition that adults with hypertension should undergo urine testing increased from 58% to 95%, knowledge that albuminuria indicates protein in the urine increased from 47% to 95%, and awareness that testing facilitates early CKD detection increased from 55% to 100% (P <0.001 for all). After the primary care visit, 77% of patients reported asking their clinician about urine testing and 65% reported that testing was ordered. EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing occurred in 36.8% of KnowCKD participants versus 11.0% of controls (risk ratio, 3.35 [95% CI, 1.96-5.73]; absolute risk difference, 25.9 percentage points [95% CI, 12.5- 39.2]). The propensity score-matched risk ratio was 2.93 (95% CI, 1.59-5.42). Participants described KnowCKD as timely, understandable, and actionable and emphasized trusted health-system communication for broader implementation. Conclusions: KnowCKD was associated with increased patient awareness of CKD and knowledge, patient engagement, and higher EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing among adults with hypertension. A rigorous evaluation of KnowCKD implementation within routine health-system workflows is warranted as a next step.

research.abstract: Objective: To identify community - prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and Methods: We combined an international, library - led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. Results: The library - led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API - mediated mapping achieving 63 - 76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community - identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. Discussion: Through a consensus - based, community - driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. Conclusion: OPEN provides a credible, community - informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

research.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

research.abstract: Objective: To assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. Methods: We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. Findings: Among 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. research.abstract: The intersection of tuberculosis (TB) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a major global health challenge. Although T2DM is a recognized risk factor for active TB, its epidemiological impact on latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and the underlying immune mechanisms remain unclear. This meta-analysis estimated the global prevalence of LTBI in T2DM, compared LTBI risk with non-diabetic controls, and evaluated the roles of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) in immune dysregulation. HbA1c and IFN-γ were selected because they represent the gold-standard indicators of long-term glycemic control and IGRA-based immune responses, respectively. A systematic search identified observational studies using interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) to diagnose LTBI in T2DM patients. Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation was performed to calculate pooled prevalence, odds ratios (ORs), mean differences (MDs) for HbA1c, and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for IFN-γ levels. Ten studies involving 1,740 T2DM patients and non-diabetic controls were included. The pooled LTBI prevalence in T2DM was 27% (95% CI: 23%–32%; I² = 76%). Compared with non-diabetic individuals, T2DM patients had an 86% higher risk of LTBI (OR 1.86; 95% CI: 1.41–2.45; p<0.0001; I² = 0%). T2DM patients with LTBI also showed poorer glycemic control, with HbA1c levels 0.75% higher than those without LTBI (MD 0.75; 95% CI: 0.51–0.99; p<0.00001; I² = 0%). Furthermore, T2DM was associated with significantly reduced Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific IFN-γ production (SMD −1.93; 95% CI: −2.69 to −1.16; p<0.00001; I² = 78%). These findings indicate that T2DM substantially increases LTBI risk through hyperglycemia-associated immune dysregulation and impaired Th1-mediated IFN-γ responses. Routine LTBI screening using IGRA and optimal glycemic control should be integrated into diabetes management to reduce progression to active TB. Keywords: : latent tuberculosis infection, type 2 diabetes mellitus, HbA1c, interferon-gamma, meta-analysis

research.abstract: Abstract Developmental programs that orchestrate cell fate and tissue architecture during organogenesis can cause disease when reactivated in adults. Here we identify a population of endothelial cells (ECs) defined by the pioneer factor early B cell factor 1 (EBF1) that controls both pulmonary artery (PA) morphogenesis and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). During embryonic development, the PA emerges from an endothelial niche harbored within the vascular plexus, where Aplnr + endothelial progenitors give rise to both arterial ECs and EBF1 + ECs. Rather than incorporating directly into the PA intima, EBF1 + ECs control the branching and maturation of the PA tree through paracrine vasculotrophic signals that direct plexus expansion, arterialization, and mural cell recruitment. Although essential for development, most EBF1 + ECs disappear upon completion of PA morphogenesis, leaving only a rare residual population within the adult Aplnr + gCap compartment. In PAH, vascular injury reactivates the EBF1 program through recruitment of the pre-existing Ebf1 lineage together with an additional contribution consistent with de novo Ebf1 induction in gCaps, reconstituting this artery-forming niche in a maladaptive reprise of PA development. Unlike their transient embryonic counterparts, these EBF1 + ECs persist within occlusive intimal lesions and express vasculotrophic signals associated with pathological PA remodeling. Combined with endothelial injury, gCap-specific Ebf1 overexpression drives a coordinated program of neo-arterialization, occlusive vascular remodeling, and severe PAH. Conversely, gCap-specific genetic deletion of Ebf1 in mice and endothelial-targeted AAV-mediated Ebf1 knockdown in rats protect against disease, showing that endothelial EBF1 is required for PAH pathogenesis. These findings demonstrate that reactivation and persistence of a transient embryonic artery-forming niche in adulthood drive pathological vascular remodeling and PAH.

research.abstract: Brandtodinium nutricula is a dinoflagellate species commonly reported in symbiosis with the marine protist host lineage, Collodaria (Rhizaria). Despite the widespread abundance of this symbiosis throughout the open ocean, and clear indications that the alga should be capable of existing outside of the symbiosis, there are no reports to date of the alga in free-living form in the environment. Even though B. nutricula molecular data are publicly available, the phylogenetic position of B. nutricula remains unclear. Our taxon-rich 18S rRNA gene phylogenetic analysis revealed a close association between B. nutricula and the copepod parasite lineage, Blastodinium. We next analyzed Tara Oceans metabarcode data to assess B. nutricula abundance outside of the Collodaria symbiosis and found that B. nutricula is common in free-living form throughout the sunlit ocean. Similarly, B. nutricula does not significantly correlate with Collodaria in terms of read depth in Tara Oceans samples, despite their tight association. We also determined that B. nutricula can live symbiotically within planktonic Foraminifera using fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy in combination with fluorescence in situ hybridization. These findings indicate that the radiolarian-B. nutricula symbiosis is less specific than previously suggested, highlighting the complexity of open ocean symbioses and the importance of weighing both host and symbiont perspectives when considering who benefits from the relationship.

research.abstract: BackgroundLimited recent data exist on prescribing patterns and patient characteristics for glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), an important drug class used as anti-diabetic medication (ADM) for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) and/or anti-obesity medication (AOM) in patients with overweight or obesity. For brevity, we use the term GLP-1 RA to refer to both GLP-1 RA and dual GLP-1 RA/GIP medications. ObjectiveTo describe recent trends in prescribing and dispensing of GLP-1-based medications in the US. MethodsUsing a subset of real-world electronic health record (EHR) data from Truveta, a growing collective of health systems that provide more than 18% of all daily clinical care in the US, we identified people who were prescribed a GLP-1-based medication between January 01, 2019 and September 30, 2026. We describe prescribing volumes and patient characteristics over time, by medication, and by FDA-labeled use. Among the subset of patients for whom post-prescription dispensing data is available, we describe the proportion and characteristics of patients who were and were not dispensed a GLP-1 RA following their prescription. AOM prescribing increased by 12.2% (+0.38 percentage points), with the largest month-over-month increase occurring from June to July and prescribing remained relatively steady thereafter. research.abstract: Abstract Freshwater biodiversity is declining at alarming rates, and the biological characteristics of small freshwater fishes make them particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation and fragmentation. Pygmy perches are small Australian fishes whose populations have recently undergone rapid declines due to human-induced pressures. They also exhibit paedomorphic miniaturization, an evolutionary phenomenon whose consequences for the persistence and diversification of freshwater fishes remain unclear. Genomic resources for pygmy perches would significantly enhance both conservation efforts and evolutionary research. Here, we describe chromosome-level genome assemblies for the Southern pygmy perch (Nannoperca australis) and the Yarra pygmy perch (N. obscura). We provide evidence for high synteny among percichthyid genomes and for positive selection on size- and growth-related genes in the pygmy perch lineage. The N. australis and N. obscura assemblies are 675.7 and 653.9 Mbp in length, with scaffold N50 values of 26.98 and 26.22 Mbp, respectively. Each assembly comprises 24 pseudo-chromosomes and 890 or 1,476 contigs, with repeat contents of 22.3% and 28.1%. We predicted 26,390 and 24,654 protein-coding genes, and BUSCO completeness scores for Teleostei genes were 96.9% and 96.5%, respectively, for N. australis and N. obscura. Their genomes are comparable in quality to the best currently available percichthyid assemblies. These genomic resources will support conservation management efforts and provide a foundation for comparative studies on the adaptive significance of miniaturization.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been instrumental in uncovering the genetic basis of complex traits. When integrated with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping, they can help identify effector genes within GWAS loci through gene regulatory mechanisms. Recent single-cell eQTL (sc-eQTL) studies suggest that genetic effects on gene expression are often cell type- and subtype-specific, offering opportunities to uncover context-specific roles of effector genes that traditional GWAS and eQTL studies in bulk tissues may obscure. Here, we leverage sc-eQTL mapping results from the TenK10K phase 1 project to prioritise effector genes across 69 diseases and 31 biomarker traits, from 12,266 eGenes identified in 28 peripheral immune cell types. Using Mendelian randomisation (MR) and colocalisation, we present a catalogue of predicted effector genes and their estimated directional effects on the trait at cell type resolution, spanning 54,245 associations across 5,270 genes and 28 cell types for disease traits, and 348,103 associations across 9,581 genes and 28 cell types for biomarker traits. By quantifying polygenic enrichment at both the single-cell and cell type levels, we identify distinct immune cell contributions to immune-related and systemic conditions. We demonstrate differential polygenic enrichment of Crohn’s disease and COVID-19 amongst dendritic cell subtypes. Integrating clinical drug development data shows that therapeutic compounds targeting the gene-trait associations identified in this study are twice as likely to secure regulatory approval. Using Crohn’s disease as a motivating example, we demonstrate how population-based sc-eQTL data can pinpoint risk loci, effector genes, and cell types, complementing findings from disease-focused tissue samples. Our findings provide a foundational resource for understanding the cell-type-specific genetic architecture of disease and for guiding therapeutic discovery.

research.abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

research.abstract: Summary The repetitive and heterochromatic parts of microchromosomes and dot chromosomes have impeded the creation of a complete, haplotype-resolved chicken genome. To overcome these challenges, we employed a trio-sequencing approach, utilizing long reads from a female chick, supplemented by parental long-read data for accurate haplotype phasing. This strategy produced nearly complete, haplotype-resolved paternal and maternal assemblies, with 14 residual gaps. Telomeric sequences remain missing in two paternal and four maternal chromosomes, suggesting a still incomplete assembly. GGswu2 resolved more than 50 Mb of previously unresolved regions, predominantly within dot chromosomes. The dot chromosomes exhibit low nucleotide diversity but a high density of structural variants between haplotypes. We found that the centromere sizes and relative positions of centromere cores sometimes differ between the two haplotype genomes. These findings suggest that comparative genomics must incorporate the high-resolution of these dynamic complex regions to fully understand avian genome evolution and genetic complexity.

research.abstract: Abstract Purpose To investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) systems detect referable diabetic retinopathy (DR) from retinal photographs by analysing heatmap patterns and determining their overlap with DR features. Methods Fifty-four AI systems were developed using 27 backbone architectures, with each implemented as both binary-referable and multi-class grading models based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading scale. Models were trained on DDR, BRSET and Kaggle datasets. After training, each model analysed 749 images with DR feature annotations, with Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP heatmaps generated and compared to pixel-level annotations of microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities and neovascularisation. Results All models achieved acceptable predictive performance (AUROC >0.8 for most architectures). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent attention to the central and temporal macular region. Exudates and cotton wool spots were highlighted most frequently by the heatmaps, with venous beading and neovascularisation at the disc showing poor overall coverage for binary referable classifiers. Models grading per the ICDR scale demonstrated higher coverage for all features. Substantial variability was observed between architectures, suggesting different feature detection capabilities. Interestingly, the heatmap analysis indicated that the models may be using different features to the ICDR grading scale definitions. Conclusion AI models do not uniformly correlate with all DR features when detecting referable DR, limiting their predictive performance in unusual presentations. Heatmap aggregation analysis provides a scalable method for analysing model behaviour, allowing strengths and weaknesses to be assessed. These findings may help improve clinician’s trust and acceptance of AI.

research.abstract: Abstract In the real world, microbes must cope with environmental fluctuations, compete for scarce resources, and avoid predation. One adaptation to survive this tangled web is the formation of multicellular aggregates, such as biofilms, which are known to be associated with pathogenicity. Despite the importance of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to biomedical research, little is known about the natural variation in its multicellular, biofilm-related traits. We investigated five multicellular phenotypes in a diverse, worldwide panel of ∼1000 isolates. We found that all traits varied significantly and ∼2/3 of the isolates expressed at least one multicellular trait. Both recent ecology and evolutionary history explained some of this variation, with clinical isolates exhibiting increased levels of three biofilm-related traits. When tested against wax moth larvae, hyper-multicellular isolates tended to be more virulent than non-multicellular isolates. Genome-wide association analysis on each trait suggested a genetic architecture of many small effect loci, compatible with polygenic adaptation. Only four genes, SLN1 , ECM5 , MLP2 , and ECM9 , were shared among the traits; deletion of MLP2 and ECM9 verified their association with multicellularity. Our results show that this yeast expresses far more multicellularity than previously appreciated and suggest that the aggregative phenotypes are likely evolving independently.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Higher resting or sleeping heart rate (HR) has been associated with poorer glucose metabolism in adults without diabetes. However, these associations were estimated across individuals, and within-person characterization of this co-regulation during naturalistic sleep in large free-living cohorts remains limited. Objective This study aimed to determine whether average sleeping HR, an indirect index of cardiac autonomic tone, is associated with nocturnal glucose within a participant and between participants, and whether night-to-night irregularity in sleep duration, sleep onset, and wake time is associated with nocturnal glycemia. Methods In this retrospective observational study, adults who concurrently wore an Ultrahuman Ring and a continuous glucose monitor between January 2024 and June 2025 were analyzed. After participant- and night-level filtering, the cohort comprised 2648 participants from 87 countries, contributing 105,196 paired nights. Each predictor was decomposed into within- and between-participant components by person-mean centering and entered a single linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept for participant, adjusted for age, body mass index (BMI), and sex. Outcomes were nocturnal mean glucose, nocturnal glucose coefficient of variation (CV), and nocturnal time in range (70-110 mg/dL). Per-participant slopes were fitted in participants with sustained wear (at least 30 nights spanning at least 60 days). Estimates were re-derived under trimming and robust-regression specifications and refitted within BMI and regional strata. Results Higher average sleeping HR was associated with higher nocturnal mean glucose both within participants (+5.7 mg/dL per 10 bpm, 95% CI 5.4-5.9) and between participants (+6.5 mg/dL, 95% CI 5.6-7.3; both P <.001). Within participants, higher sleeping HR was also associated with higher glucose CV (+1.37 percentage points, 95% CI 1.30-1.43) and lower time in range (−6.3 percentage points, 95% CI −6.7 to −6.0). Of the 911 sustained-wear participants, 701 (76.9%, 95% CI 74.1%-79.6%) had a positive individual slope (median of +5.2 mg/dL per 10 bpm). The association survived in every BMI stratum and in all 5 regional strata. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with mean glucose between participants (+4.1 mg/dL per 30 minutes, 95% CI 2.6-5.7) but only weakly within them (+0.23 mg/dL). Within participants, a night 1 standard deviation above a participant’s own mean sleeping HR corresponded to 2.5 mg/dL higher nocturnal mean glucose. Conclusions Average sleeping HR was associated with glucose within individuals as well as between them, indicating that the relationship is not attributable solely to stable between-person differences and reflects, at least in part, night-to-night covariation. The association was modest, but discernible in naturalistic sleep across geographies. Sleep-duration irregularity was associated with nocturnal glycemia mainly between individuals.

research.abstract: Abstract The distribution of fitness effects (DFE) describes the proportion of new mutations with certain selective strengths. It is a crucial quantity for the study of complex disease and evolutionary genetics. Population genetics approaches infer the DFE using the site frequency spectrum (SFS), which summarizes allele frequencies within a sample. These approaches first fit a demographic model to an SFS of putatively neutral sites, then infer the DFE from an SFS of selected sites conditional on that demographic model. This approach assumes that sites are independent and that population size changes affect selected and neutral sites equally. Selective sweeps may violate these assumptions. As a beneficial mutation rises in frequency, nearby sites hitchhike alongside the beneficial mutation. This distortion might differ between neutral and selected sites.. Here, we evaluate the performance of the DFE inference method, fit∂ a ∂ i , in the presence of selective sweeps. We simulate genomic segments containing neutral and deleterious mutations drawn from a known DFE under varying selective sweep conditions, and test whether fit∂ a ∂ i can recover the true DFE with a flexible demographic model. When SFS are sampled immediately after fixation of a beneficial mutation, the demographic models absorb the sweep’s effect as a population expansion, and the DFE is recovered relatively well. Performance declines at lower recombination rates and when using the unfolded SFS, leading to an overestimation of the strength of purifying selection. We then model recurrent selective sweeps at rates consistent with human polymorphism and divergence data. The demographic model captures these distortions, and the DFE is unbiased. Our results suggest that DFE inferences are unlikely to be substantially biased by selective sweeps, but that future studies should consider using the folded SFS and excluding regions of low recombination rate.

research.abstract: Abstract Multiple classes of selfish genetic elements, including transposable elements, meiotic drivers, and viruses, are suppressed by small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that guide RNA interference (RNAi). These are interlocked within continually evolving genetic conflicts that are characterized by extremely rapid dynamics of change in both sequence and copy number. Indeed, it was shown that across Drosophila , the core RNAi machinery evolves under positive selection, and that the RNAi effector AGO2 has additional copies in some species. This contrasts with the core microRNA (miRNA) machinery in Drosophila , which evolves under negative selection and maintains one-to-one orthologs not only amongst flies, but even to mammals. Here, we analyze >300 long read genome assemblies of Drosophila species to generalize these attributes. Not only do we find recurrent expansion of AGO2 across ∼100 species, including lineages with ongoing amplification of AGO2, we also find dozens of species with extra copies of the other core RNAi factors, r2d2 and dicer-2 . In many cases, these additional RNAi factor copies co-exist, or are nested, within a lineage bearing an ancestral expansion of AGO2 . Transcriptome data provide evidence that core RNAi factors, including certain lineage-specific copies, are biased for testis expression. Finally, we use small RNA data to annotate hairpin RNAs (hpRNAs) in D. pseudoobscura , one of the species with prominent amplification of RNAi factors. We find rampant de novo hpRNA loci in this species, whose siRNAs are predominantly expressed in testis. All together, these findings highlight evolutionary plasticity of the fly RNAi pathway and affirm that it is preferentially deployed in the germline of the heterogametic sex. When considered alongside abundant genetic data for recurrent sex ratio meiotic drive against the Y chromosome, these genomic data strongly imply that a fundamental role of endogenous RNAi is to control sex chromosome conflicts.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), represents an important cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide for which an improved vaccine and immunodiagnostics are urgently needed. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells play an important role in host defense to TB. Definition of the immunodominant antigens recognized by these T cells is critical for improved understanding of the immunobiology of TB and for development of vaccines and diagnostics. Herein, we review antigens and epitopes recognized by classically human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I- and class II-restricted CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in humans infected with MTB, as defined using either targeted or genome-wide approaches. We address the extent to which these antigens have been defined as immunodominant, protective, and/or specific to disease stages in humans and, with particular relevance to CD8+ T-cell recognition, whether these antigens are displayed by MTB-infected cells.

research.abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of single-nucleotide variant (SNV) tolerability across the entire human genome remains a fundamental challenge in computational genomics, particularly for non-coding regions where the regulatory landscape is vast and poorly understood. Machine learning classifiers suffer from data circularity and demographic bias, while genomic language models demand massive computational resources and offer little biological interpretability. Here, we present PHACTn (Phylogeny-Aware Computing of Tolerance for nucleotide variants), a training-free, parameter-minimal method that infers nucleotide variant tolerability by traversing the mammalian phylogenetic tree and explicitly modeling the evolutionary independence of observed substitutions and their distance from the query species. With only 4 interpretable parameters, no training and no GPU requirement, PHACTn outperforms all evaluated tools on non-coding variants curated from both the ClinVar, and on non-coding variants potentially responsible for selected Mendelian diseases curated from OMIM. Additionally, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on variants within the informative range of alignment-based inference. These results establish that principled probabilistic phylogenetic modeling captures evolutionary constraint signals that large-scale sequence models fail to recover, offering a powerful, accessible, and mechanistically transparent alternative for genome-wide variant effect prediction.

research.abstract: Abstract The thymus enacts central tolerance through thymic epithelial cells (TECs), which present self-antigens to developing T cells to remove self-reactive cells, preventing autoimmunity. Human TECs include populations that express lineage-committed programs corresponding to distinct peripheral tissues, yet how they acquire these programs and whether these TEC subpopulations are genetically related and conserved in mice remain unknown. Using matched single-cell gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiling of 126,687 human TECs, we identified 17 TEC subsets defined by their distinct expression profiles of 1,843 cell type restricted-antigens (CRAs) from 48 peripheral cell types. With a new phylogenetic reconstruction method, we show that lineage-committed TECs share a common ancestor, retain a thymus-specific mixed identity through co-expression of multiple CRA signatures, and are specified by coordinated activator and repressor regulons. We also identified a basement-membrane-collagen-rich state (BMC-TECs) with progenitor-like properties. Finally, mouse TECs shared the regulatory strategy but conserved few master transcription-factor drivers. This study mechanistically characterizes human TEC subpopulations and reveals the gene regulatory logic that leads to their distinct diversification and mixed identities in humans and mice.

Its genomic diversity remains undescribed in Sénégal where M. africanum was first described and where the present study was conducted. RESULTS: Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) identified one M. africanum lineage L5 isolate and 50 M. africanum lineage L6 isolates, with a predominance of sub lineage L6.1.1 (24/50, 43.7%) across seven of eight regions of Sénégal. The Dakar region gathered all the sub lineages (L5.3, L6.1, L6.1.1, L6.1.3, L6.2.3, L6.3.1, L6.3.2, L6.3.3, unclassified L6), except for sub lineage L6.2. Further Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) analysis revealed substantial genetic diversity among the lineage L6 isolates with mean value of 668.54 (±239.61), while themedian was 465 SNPs (interquartile range = 400, median absolute deviation:163.09). According to the World health Organization Catalogue of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance, WGS predicted antibiotic resistance in 16 strains. Comparing Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST) and WGS results showed complete concordance across 19 DST tested strains. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the diversity of M. africanum in Sénégal, with intra-lineage genomic variability and predicted antimicrobial resistance. The presence of synonymous mutations in the absence of resistance-associated variants suggests that WGS-based predictions of drug resistance should be interpreted with caution.

research.abstract: The B3 superfamily is one of the largest plant transcription factor gene families, yet its evolutionary dynamics in dioecious species like Cannabis sativa remain largely unexplored. Here, we present a comprehensive phylogenetic, molecular evolution, and transcriptomic analysis of B3 domain-containing genes in Arabidopsis thaliana , C. sativa , and Humulus lupulus . Using a gene mining pipeline, we identified 110, 101, and 88 B3 genes across the five established subfamilies ( ARF , ABI3 , HSI , RAV , and REM), respectively. We identified two distinct evolutionary trajectories with the B3 superfamily. On the one hand the REM subfamily was by far the largest and characterized by massive lineage-specific tandem duplications subjected to relaxed selective constraint, suggesting distinct or partially redundant roles in reproductive development. On the other hand, specific non-tandem clades remained highly conserved under strong purifying selection. Detailed analysis of the candidate sex-determination gene CsREM16 showed low dN/dS ratios, clear one-to-one orthology across studied species, and unique persistent sex-biased expression across all six analyzed developmental stages in C. sativa . Comparative analysis of its ortholog HlREM16 confirmed a conserved female-biased expression in H. lupulus . Together, these results demonstrate a dual-mode evolutionary dynamic in the B3 superfamily and particularly in the REM genes and establish CsREM16 as a strong candidate for sex determination in C. sativa , with a potentially conserved role in H. lupulus .

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Purpose Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. Methods We performed systematic searches in seven databases until July 2026. We included observational studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the TB score to diagnosis of TB across different clinical contexts. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Meta-analysis was performed using the logit function, and GRADE was employed to assess certainty of evidence (CoE). Results Twenty-eight studies were included. For distinguishing pulmonary TB from other respiratory diseases, the TB score showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84) and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64-0.78), respectively, with an AUC of 0.82. When comparing pulmonary TB to healthy controls, sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity was 0.86, with an AUC of 0.87. Performance was lower for meningeal tuberculosis (sensitivity 0.58; specificity 0.67) and for distinguishing active from latent TB (sensitivity 0.73; specificity 0.76). Risk of bias was generally low. The CoE for most outcomes was very low. Conclusion The TB score shows moderate diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary TB, with pooled sensitivity below the WHO TPP minimum for a standalone triage test. High heterogeneity and very low CoE limit confidence in these findings. Its potential role as a complementary tool remains investigational and requires validation in prospective studies.

research.abstract: Abstract Mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs) have been extensively studied in cancer and clonal hematopoiesis but less so in healthy solid tissues. Here, we characterized mCAs in 19 tissues across 25 donors (aged 42–89+ years) by analyzing >200x whole-genome sequencing data generated by the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network. Across 722 tissue samples, we identified 1,008 autosomal mCAs >1 Mb in length and ubiquitous losses of sex chromosomes. Surprisingly, the highest levels of Y chromosome loss in males (5–10% cell fraction in elderly donors) were observed in the lung, adrenal gland, and heart. These tissues also tended to experience more X loss in females, revealing a gradient of mitotic error burden across human tissues. Autosomal aneuploidies displayed distinct tissue-specific patterns indicative of negative selection against most events, except in the adrenal gland, in which low-level aneuploidy was pervasive. In contrast to the adrenal gland, testis rarely harbored aneuploidies but frequently experienced low-level copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), suggesting increased mitotic recombination in spermatogonial stem cells. Recurrent X chromosome losses within tissues of female donors exhibited allelic skews explained by a combination of genetic and epigenetic effects. Together, these results show that the chromosomal landscape of aging human tissues is shaped by genetics and recurrent mutations, most but not all of which are held in check by purifying selection.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Synonymous substitution rates in the coding regions of land plant mitochondrial genomes are substantially lower than those in the nucleus. In contrast, non-coding regions are difficult or impossible to align except among very closely related species, suggesting that point mutation rates in these regions are considerably higher. Rearrangement breakpoints occur frequently within non-coding DNA, generating duplications, deletions, and inversions. To reconcile these contradictory patterns of genome evolution, it has been proposed that DNA damage is converted into double-strand breaks that are repaired through a combination of template-directed mechanisms and non-homologous end joining, while purifying selection preserves the integrity of coding sequences. Here we characterized AtSUV3 , a mitochondrially targeted RNA helicase encoded by Arabidopsis thaliana At4g14790, a gene previously proposed to function as part of the plant mitochondrial degradosome. Mutations in AtSUV3 confer hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin-induced mitochondrial DNA damage, CRISPR-knockout lines display increased ectopic recombination in the mitochondrial genome, and recombinant AtSUV3 exhibits ATP-dependent RNA helicase activity with a preference for 3′-ended substrates. Together, these findings identify AtSUV3 as a factor involved in mitochondrial dsDNA break repair. Consistent with our results, Arabidopsis and other plants encode an uncharacterized gene, AT5G39840.1, with 75% amino acid similarity with AtSUV3, dubbed herein as SUV3-like. We hypothesize that the AtSUV3 paralog has undergone specialization towards DNA repair, whereas AtSUV3-like protein may play a role in the plant organellar degradosome. Collectively, these findings identify AtSUV3 as a previously unrecognized factor involved in mitochondrial dsDNA break repair and provide a framework for understanding the diversification of DNA repair proteins during plant evolution. research.abstract: Abstract Gene duplication is a major source of evolutionary novelty, but duplicated genes do not share a single fate. We compared the duplication history of the Hedgehog ligand and its receptor Patched across land snails and slugs (Stylommatophora), a group with a debated ancestral whole-genome duplication. In eleven genomes, Hedgehog and Patched are each retained in two copies, whereas Smoothened is strictly single-copy. The two Hedgehog paralogs form two deeply separated clades; one evolves under consistently relaxed constraint, accumulating amino-acid substitutions faster in all ten species (median ratio 1.86), with a higher dN /dS (0.222 versus 0.156) and shorter introns. The two Patched copies are both strongly constrained (ω 0.116 and 0.126). At the site level, the Hedgehog copies show significant rate-shift (Type I) divergence concentrated in the C-terminal Hog domain, whereas the Patched copies show none. The genomic contexts differ too. In two Cepaea species the Patched paralogs lie on a chromosome-scale duplicate pair retaining 74–95% two-sided collinear coverage, and their neighbourhoods stay syntenic in eight of nine genomes; the Hedgehog pair retains 20% and 53%, and its neighbourhood test is significant in one of eight. Hedgehog collinearity is reduced but not absent; the data do not distinguish a different mechanism from faster local evolution. Two public Hedgehog models are defective, and Gli, reported as single-copy from proteomes, has a second partially degenerated copy in Lissachatina immaculata. Proteome-level inventories alone are an unreliable guide to copy number.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Species inhabiting high-elevation environments face energetic and physiological challenges, creating opportunities for adaptive divergence from lowland taxa. The yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), a Critically Endangered primate endemic to high-elevation forests in Andean Perú, provides a unique system for investigating the evolutionary consequences of long-term occupation of high elevations. We used Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) to generate a high-coverage mitochondrial reference genome using low-quality fecal samples. Using this and a new mitogenome from a closely-related lowland common woolly monkey (L. lagotricha poeppigii), we estimated divergence dates and calculated substitution ratios to investigate the evolutionary history of both Lagothrix taxa and assess whether high-elevation living has left signatures of selection in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes of L. flavicauda. RESULTS: We assembled a high-coverage (9190X) reference mitogenome of 16,603 bp for L. flavicauda from a 15-year-old fecal sample, and a novel mitogenome for L. lagotricha poeppigii from fresh tissue (112X, 16,590 bp). Our phylogenetic reconstruction is consistent with other platyrrhine primate phylogenies with high bootstrap support, with the two Lagothrix taxa showing evidence of having diverged from one another ~ 2.8 million years ago. Substitution (d N /d S) ratios suggest purifying selection on protein-coding mitogenomic regions in all assessed lineages. CONCLUSIONS: We found no evidence of positive selection acting on mitochondrial protein-coding genes in either L. flavicauda or the broader genus Lagothrix; all analyses instead support pervasive purifying selection across genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. These results suggest that unlike in some other non-human primates occupying high elevations, the adaptive response of L. flavicauda to living in the Andes does not appear to involve evolution in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathway, and likely involves alternative genetic pathways or mechanisms not captured by mitochondrial sequence evolution. By providing the first publicly available high-coverage mitochondrial genome for L. flavicauda, this study establishes a foundation for future population mitogenomic investigations of adaptation, evolutionary history, and conservation in this Critically Endangered, high-altitude primate.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Glucagon-like peptide-1receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are increasingly used to treat diabetes mellitus (DM) and obesity. However, their impact on the progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) among those with comorbid DM is unknown. Objective We examined the relationship between GLP-1RA treatment and disease progression among people with ALS and DM. Methods This multicenter retrospective chart review study used an electronic health record search at 14 institutions to identify consecutive patients with a confirmed ALS diagnosis and documented comorbid type 1 or type 2 DM. All charts were reviewed for demographics, disease history, medication use, and tracheostomy/survival status. Patients who did not meet Awaji ALS diagnostic criteria, lacked a documented history of DM, or had insufficient records were excluded. Tracheostomy-free survival was compared between the GLP-1RA group (exposed) and No-GLP-1RA group (unexposed) using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age and region of onset (bulbar, respiratory, and diffuse, versus spinal). Results A total of 308 ALS patients with comorbid DM were included from 14 institutions, of whom 39 (13%) were treated with one or more GLP-1RA. In the GLP-1RA group, diagnostic delay was shorter (10.2 vs 15.9 months, p<0.001), and revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) score decline from symptom onset to first measure was faster (1.5 vs 1.1 points/month, p=0.023) compared with the No-GLP-1RA group. Other baseline characteristics, including age, sex, race, region of onset, and first ALSFRS-R score, were not significantly different between groups. Tracheostomy-free survival from symptom onset was numerically shorter in the GLP-1RA group (median survival 27.0 vs 36.7 months; log-rank p=0.073). After adjusting for age and region of onset, GLP-1RA exposure was associated with an increased risk of tracheostomy or death (hazard ratio 1.56, 95% confidence interval 1.06-2.28, p=0.024). Conclusions In this multicenter cohort, GLP-1RA treatment was associated with faster disease progression and shorter tracheostomy-free survival in people with ALS and comorbid DM.

research.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis contact investigation (TBCI) facilitates early detection of TB among household contacts. However, evidence on the additional contribution of repeat TBCI in high-burden settings remains limited. We assessed the contribution of repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months to TB case detection in Kasama District, Zambia. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort analysis of routinely collected programme data from five purposively selected high-volume TB diagnostic facilities. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients notified between January 2023 and April 2024 underwent symptom-based TB screening at baseline and at 6 and 12 months. We estimated round-specific TB detection yields, the cumulative proportion diagnosed with TB, and the contribution of repeat investigations to overall case detection. Results: Among 1,250 index TB patients, 3,648 household contacts were identified and screened at baseline. TB was diagnosed in 143 (3.9%) contacts at baseline, 31 (0.9%) at month 6, and 25 (0.7%) at month 12. Overall, 199 (5.5%) contacts were diagnosed with TB across the three screening rounds, of whom 159 (79.9%) had bacteriologically confirmed disease. Repeat investigations identified 56 additional cases, representing 28.1% of all TB diagnoses. Conclusions: Repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months identified additional TB cases beyond baseline screening, although detection yields declined across successive rounds. These findings support further evaluation of risk-based follow-up strategies and more sensitive baseline screening approaches to optimize TB case detection and resource utilization in high-burden settings.

research.abstract: Background Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) species are common healthcare-associated pathogens that cause difficult-to-treat infections. Whole genome sequencing of patients has revealed a substantial burden of patient-to-patient VRE transmission in hospitals, with patients in intensive care units (ICUs) at particularly high risk of acquisition. However, few studies adequately characterize the pathways of VRE transmission between patients in acute care settings - a necessary step to identify current gaps in infection prevention practices. By harnessing genomic clustering analyses of whole genome sequences of VRE isolates from patients, environmental surfaces, and healthcare providers (HCP) in ICUs, we aim to reconstruct indirect pathways of pathogen movement to identify patterns of VRE spread and opportunities for transmission prevention. Methods and Findings We collected daily samples (N = 6848) from ICUs in two hospitals over 13 weeks from four main sampling sources: patients, HCP hands, patient rooms, and shared surfaces. Samples were cultured on selective media and sent for whole genome sequencing (WGS). We used genomic thresholds to identify clusters of related VRE isolates and distinguish unrelated isolates. VRE was detected in samples from 20 out of 322 unique occupant-stays (6.22%). VRE isolates were detected from all sampling sources except for shared surfaces. A total of 44 unique VRE isolates were identified, 43 Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and one Enterococcus faecalis (VREf). Two distinct patterns of VREfm spread were observed: 1) an outbreak setting with observed patient-to-patient transmission and low VRE genomic heterogeneity, and 2) high VRE genomic heterogeneity and pathogen movement between occupant-stays facilitated by persistent HCP and environmental contamination, but no observed transmission events. VRE detection probabilities were not significantly different between occupant-stays in outbreak and non-outbreak settings (OR = 0.63, 95% CI (0.23, 1.83), p = 0.32). However, including VRE isolates from non-patient samples increased the number of occupant-stays with VRE detection from 6 to 20, a 3.3-fold increase, as compared to patient samples alone. Including non-patient samples also increased the number of VRE multi-isolate genomic clusters detected by 7-fold. Our findings are limited because sampling was primarily conducted in ICUs. Due to the combination of short ICU stay durations and imperfect test sensitivity, VRE transmission events may have been underdetected. Conclusions Our findings characterize the complex nature of VRE transmission pathways in ICU settings. Even without an ongoing outbreak, we found substantial evidence of VRE movement between occupant-stays, facilitated by a combination of HCP hands and environmental surfaces. This study highlights the importance of environmental sampling for understanding VRE transmission potential, which is likely to be underestimated using patient sampling alone. We recommend that future studies incorporate follow-up sampling after discharge to better understand the true burden of transmission.
